keyTakeaways: There is no single right age to stop trick or treating; most families land between 12 and 15 and judge behavior over birthday.
Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Hampton, Newport News and Portsmouth, Virginia still ban trick-or-treating over age 12 in their 2026 code supplements.
Chesapeake raised its cap from over 12 to over 14 on 12 March 2019 and dropped a 1970 clause allowing up to six months in jail.
In YouGov's 2021 poll of 1,000 US adults, about one in four said a child is never too old, and no single age drew more than 12%.

faqs.question: Is 13 too old to trick-or-treat?
faqs.answer: Not by most people's standards: in YouGov's 2021 poll only 11% of US adults picked 13 as the age kids become too old. It is, though, the first banned age under the codes of Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Hampton, Newport News and Portsmouth, Virginia, which all cap trick-or-treating at over 12.

faqs.question: Is 16 too old to go trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: Many adults would say yes, but about one in four Americans told YouGov a child can never be too old. At 16 it works best as a costumed group that lets little kids go first and finishes by 8 pm, or as a helper role at your own door.

faqs.question: Can you get in trouble for trick-or-treating at 14 in Virginia?
faqs.answer: It depends on the city. In Chesapeake, 14 is still allowed because the cap is over 14, but in Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Hampton and Newport News it is a Class 4 misdemeanor with a fine of up to $250 and no jail term. Portsmouth makes it a Class 3 misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $500.

faqs.question: What did Chesapeake change about its trick-or-treating law in 2019?
faqs.answer: Ordinance 19-O-038, passed on 12 March 2019, raised the cap from over 12 to over 14 and made both offenses Class 4 misdemeanors. The 1970 text it replaced allowed a fine of $25 to $100, up to six months in jail, or both.

faqs.question: Can parents walk with their kids in a town that has an age limit?
faqs.answer: Yes. All six Hampton Roads codes we read let a parent, guardian or other responsible person accompany a child under the cap. Newport News adds that the accompanying adult may not wear a mask of any type.

faqs.question: What time does trick-or-treating end?
faqs.answer: There is no national rule. The six Virginia city codes we read all make trick-or-treating after 8 pm an offense, and many other towns publish their own hours each October, so check your local council's notice.

faqs.question: Do adults go trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: Some do, and younger adults are the most relaxed about it. In YouGov's October 2021 poll, 41% of 18- to 29-year-olds said nobody is ever too old, against 14% of people aged 65 and over.

faqs.question: Should an older child with a learning disability still trick-or-treat?
faqs.answer: If they enjoy it, yes, and a parent walking alongside helps neighbors read the situation. None of the six Virginia codes we read has a disability exception, so in those cities going together is the practical answer.

faqs.question: How do I tell my kid this is their last Halloween trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: Tell them in September, not on the night, and let them plan the final run: route, friends and costume. Give them a new role for next year, so it feels like a graduation rather than a ban.

faqs.question: When is Halloween in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is always 31 October. It falls on a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027.

# What Age to Stop Trick or Treating: Laws, Polls and a Fair Rule

There is no single age to stop trick or treating, and in most places no law sets one; the honest family rule is somewhere between 12 and 15, decided by behavior rather than birthday. A few city codes do draw a line, and five in Virginia still set it at 12 in their 2026 code supplements. If this is a child's final year at the door, mark it: on SubhSandesh 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page is viewed 11.1 times on average (platform-wide figures, not Halloween data). Below: the code text, what a 1,000-person poll found, teen etiquette and how to end it well. Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

## What does "too old to trick-or-treat" actually mean?

"Too old to trick-or-treat" is a social norm, not a legal status, except in the handful of towns that wrote an age into their code. It usually describes the point at which neighbors stop reading a visitor as a child collecting sweets and start reading them as a teenager taking them.

A small 14-year-old in full costume reads very differently from a 6-foot 13-year-old in a hoodie, which is why most parents judge effort and manners rather than age.

## Which places have a trick-or-treating age limit?

We read the current text of six Hampton Roads, Virginia city codes on Municode on 15 October 2026. All six set an age cap and an 8 pm finish and let a parent walk with a younger child; each entry gives the cap, penalty and when the text last changed.

### 1. Chesapeake: over 14 (rewritten 2019)

[Chesapeake's City Code § 46-8](https://library.municode.com/va/chesapeake/codes/code_of_ordinances?nodeId=PTIICOOR_CH46OFMIPR_ARTIINGE_S46-8TRTRAC) makes trick-or-treating by anyone over 14 a Class 4 misdemeanor, and trick-or-treating by anyone after 8 pm the same. The current wording comes from Ordinance 19-O-038, passed 12 March 2019.

The version in force until then, dating from an ordinance of 26 October 1970, capped it at over 12. It carried a fine of $25 to $100, up to six months in jail, or both, which is the clause behind years of "teens could be jailed" headlines.

### 2. Norfolk: over 12

Norfolk's § 29-4 still bans trick-or-treating by anyone over 12 and by anyone after 8 pm, each a Class 4 misdemeanor. A parent or guardian may accompany a child of 12 or younger.

The section cites the 1958 city code and lists no later amendment, and the June 2026 supplement carries it unchanged.

### 3. Virginia Beach: over 12

Virginia Beach's § 23-3 uses near-identical words: over 12 is a Class 4 misdemeanor, as is any trick-or-treating after 8 pm. The accompanying-adult exception again stops at 12.

Its history note points to Ordinance 1660 of 27 October 1986, and the May 2026 supplement still reads over 12.

### 4. Hampton: over 12

Hampton's § 24-5 sets the same over-12 cap and 8 pm limit, both Class 4 misdemeanors. What stands out is the date: the section was amended by Ordinance 16-0016 on 26 October 2016.

So the city revisited the rule within the last decade and kept 12.

### 5. Newport News: over 12, or past seventh grade

Newport News's § 28-5 bans anyone "beyond the seventh grade of school or over twelve (12) years of age", so a young eighth-grader is caught too. Both offenses are Class 4 misdemeanors.

It adds one rule no other code here has: an accompanying parent or guardian may not wear a mask of any type.

### 6. Portsmouth: over 12, the stiffest penalty

[Portsmouth's § 24-4](https://library.municode.com/va/portsmouth/codes/code_of_ordinances?nodeId=PTIICO_CH24OFMIPR_ARTIINGE_S24-4TRTRAC) sets the over-12 cap and the 8 pm limit as Class 3 misdemeanors, one class higher than its neighbors. It traces to the city's 1973 code.

Under [Virginia Code § 18.2-11](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title18.2/chapter1/section18.2-11/), a Class 3 misdemeanor carries a fine of up to $500 and a Class 4 up to $250, with no jail term for either. We found no published count of how often any of these sections is enforced.

## What do polls say is the right age?

The most-quoted poll is [YouGov's October 2021 survey of 1,000 US adult citizens](https://today.yougov.com/society/articles/38968-do-americans-actually-like-halloween), fielded 8 to 12 October 2021 on an opt-in panel and weighted to the population. About one in four said a child can never be too old, 12% picked 12 as the age kids become too old, 11% picked 13, 8% picked 14 and 7% picked 15.

Age split the answer sharply. Among adults aged 18 to 29, 41% said never too old, against 14% of those 65 and over; the same poll found 21% of adults will pretend not to be home when trick-or-treaters knock.

The table lines those answers up against the six city codes. We hold no Halloween usage data, so there is no first-party column.

| First age counted "too old" | Share of US adults who chose it (YouGov, Oct 2021) | City codes drawing the line here (of 6 read, Oct 2026) | Usual US school year at that age |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 12% | 0 | 6th to 7th grade |
| 13 | 11% | 5 (Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Hampton, Newport News, Portsmouth) | 7th to 8th grade |
| 14 | 8% | 0 | 8th to 9th grade |
| 15 | 7% | 1 (Chesapeake) | 9th to 10th grade |
| Never too old | about 1 in 4 | 0 | Any |

The takeaway: only 23% of adults chose 12 or 13, the ages at or below the five Virginia caps, and no single age drew more than 12%.

## Is a teenager who still wants candy a problem?

Usually not. A study in Child Development by Joseph Allen and colleagues followed 184 adolescents from age 13 to 23 and found that [early "pseudomature" behavior predicted later trouble](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4165811): difficulties in close relationships, problems with alcohol and other substances, and more criminal behavior. We read the abstract only.

That study did not look at Halloween. It does suggest a 13-year-old rushing to look grown-up is a bigger worry than a 14-year-old happily knocking on doors in a homemade costume.

The practical test is behavior: a teen who dresses up, waits behind younger children and says thank you is still playing the game.

## Teen trick-or-treating etiquette: 5 house rules

If your 13- to 15-year-old is still going, these five rules keep neighbors friendly. The 8 pm finish matches every code we read.

- Wear a real costume. Face paint and a cape count; a hoodie and a mask do not.
- Let little ones go first, and step back from the step so a four-year-old is not facing a crowd of teenagers.
- Say "trick or treat" and "thank you", every door, out loud.
- Take one piece unless offered more, and compliment a good decoration on the way out.
- Be home by 8 pm, earlier on a school night.

If your teen would rather do something else entirely, that is a different question from age, and a fine answer too.

## How do you tell a child it's their last year?

Anthropologist Arnold van Gennep described rites of passage in three stages: separation, transition and incorporation. A 2018 paper by Janusz and Walkiewicz in the Journal of Adult Development argues [those rites create clearly marked boundaries](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6105198) and new social roles. A last Halloween at the door is a tiny version of that: it goes better as an announced ending with a new role after it than as a quiet "you're too old now".

Four ways to make the final lap feel like a graduation rather than a ban:

- Tell them in September, not on 31 October, so the last year is something to plan rather than a surprise.
- Let them choose the route, the friends and the costume for the final run.
- Put the first and last costume photos side by side and keep the last bucket on a shelf.
- Agree what next year looks like, such as handing out candy at your own door with a costume still on.

Or skip the ending altogether: if your town has no cap and your child still loves it at 15, about one adult in four would cheer them on.

## A Halloween card to mark the last trick-or-treat

A small keepsake helps the "graduation" land: the [Halloween card in Kids mode](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) suits a 12- or 13-year-old: it takes up to six photos, so the first and last costumes can sit together, takes about five minutes, and the Kids tone keeps it spooky-cute with no gore and a No button that waits as "maybe later?".

For an older teen who would roll their eyes at cute, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) holds up to 12 photos and a voice note of up to 60 seconds, and you can set an unlock time so it opens after they get home. It has a reply box, so they can answer in up to 280 characters. 90.9% of pages started on SubhSandesh are published and shared, and 38.5% of creators add a password, which is worth doing for a page full of a child's photos.

Not a Halloween kid? [Browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) instead.

## When a hard age rule, or our card, is the wrong choice

A strict number is the wrong tool for a child with a developmental disability who looks older than they are. None of the six codes we read carves out an exception for that; each only lets a parent walk with a younger child, so in those cities the honest advice is to go with them and expect the occasional raised eyebrow.

Our card is wrong when the child would rather keep going, because a "last year" keepsake can feel like a verdict. It is also an English-only, one-person greeting page, and we hold no data on how children respond to Halloween pages.
